features.description: rEdit speaks the Language Server Protocol: a project declares its language servers, the workspace worker runs them and keeps their documents in sync with the editor's buffers, and their diagnostics reach both the editor pane and getDiagnostics — so an agent asks the editor what is broken and gets the same answer the person is looking at.
acceptance_criteria: A project declares its language servers by command and by the file patterns each serves; nothing is downloaded or installed by rEngine, and an undeclared project keeps answering an empty diagnostic list rather than guessing at a server.

The worker owns the server processes and the LSP session: initialize with the workspace roots, textDocument/didOpen, didChange and didClose driven by what the editor actually has open, and shutdown when the last document closes or the worker retires, leaving no orphaned server process.

Document sync carries the editor's unsaved buffer, not the file on disk, so diagnostics describe what the person is looking at; positions cross the boundary as UTF-16 line and character, which is what the protocol counts, verified against tabs and multi-byte characters.

publishDiagnostics reaches two consumers from one store: the editor pane renders them, and mcp__ide__getDiagnostics answers with the same set for a file, so the agent and the person never disagree about what is broken. MET: the pane asks the worker twice a second, is answered `unchanged` almost every time, and draws an underline under each reported range coloured by severity; the same store answers mcp__ide__getDiagnostics. LIMIT, recorded rather than glossed: the spec asserts the count the pane holds and that it stays held, not the cells the underline lands on — the draw loop's own column tracking is exercised on every frame but not asserted positionally.
A server that crashes is restarted with a bounded backoff, its diagnostics are cleared rather than left stale, and repeated failure is reported instead of retried forever.

Parsed output from a declared check action remains a second source merged into the same store, distinguishable by origin, because a build reports failures no language server sees. NOT MET: the second source is not built; only the protocol's own diagnostics are served.

The replacement is started detached, with no inherited pipes, so it survives the pane that asked for it — which is normally a pane inside the workspace being restarted, whose window the restart closes.
The launcher is invoked without --replace-host, adopting the running host rather than ending its sessions; the absence of that flag is asserted.
The report names the host it kept and each supervisor it stopped, including how many desktop windows close with it, so a vanishing editor window is predicted rather than surprising.
It is reachable as a declared dashboard action, opening as a retained interactive script tab like every other action, and it asks for confirmation before signalling anything.

Each regression was observed failing for its own reason: the host added to the stop list, the replacement left attached, --replace-host added to the launcher, and the plan computed after stopping had begun.

Every criterion above is met including the live run, but this row stays passes: false because its prerequisite F94 (--replace-host, whose process-table helpers this is built on) is not itself verified. The dependency is real rather than bookkeeping: the refusals that keep the session host safe are F94's code.

features.description: An extension is an in-process native plugin (charter D38): a module built against one C header loads by absolute path, negotiates its ABI and draw-list versions, registers tabs through the owned layer and draws by appending to the frame's draw list — and a module that will not load, exports no entry point or declares an incompatible ABI is refused by name while the window keeps running.
acceptance_criteria: A plugin built against orchestrator/native/plugin_abi.h loads from its absolute module path in a real window; the tab it registered appears in the layout with its title, and its draw-list commands reach the frame — the identifiable colour it draws is read back from a snapshot inside the tab's rectangle.

The ABI is versioned separately from the draw list and a plugin declares both: an ABI version other than the desktop's — older or newer — is refused naming the module path and both versions, and its start is never called; a newer draw-list version is refused the same way and an older one is accepted, because the list is additive (spec 067).

A declaration whose abi string is not this desktop's is refused before the module file is touched; a path that will not open, a file that is not a module, a relative path, a module without re_plugin_entry, a descriptor whose name disagrees with the declaration, and a start that declines are each refused by name and skipped, and the window keeps answering and rendering afterwards.

Every plugin the window was asked to load has a row in the inspected state as loaded or refused with its reason; loading the same name twice is one plugin and one tab, so a declaration that arrives repeatedly does not touch the module again.

A plugin's frame opens with the clip set to its tab's area, a clip it sets can only narrow that area, the frame closes with a clip reset whatever the plugin did, registration outside start is refused, and a theme colour is resolved by token name from the live theme so a preset switch reaches the plugin on the next frame.

A plugin tab is persisted by identity like any other view: a restarted window restores it as a placeholder naming the plugin, and the same tab — not a second one — comes alive when the plugin loads again.

The plugin reaches no store, session or host state: the host table it receives holds registration, drawing, clipping, measurement and colour lookup and nothing else (D38). Controls, textures, input, a reopen menu and unloading are deferred with their reasons in spec 106.

NOT MET — Windows: the loader compiles to LoadLibrary/GetProcAddress and the fixture modules build as DLLs from the same TOML, but no plugin has been loaded on Windows while the desktop suite's repair (KI-038) is outstanding. This row stays passes: false until that evidence exists.
Each regression was observed failing for its own reason: the sabotage table in docs/evidence/plugin-abi-2026-09-07.md.

features.description: A pack is one pinned, versioned artifact a project declares, and its facets say how it is consumed: contract 9 adds a packs block whose library facet is source and a CMake target a game consumes at build time and whose plugin facet is a module the editor loads at run time, with "Powered by rEngine" checkable on the library facet alone.
acceptance_criteria: A contract-9 declaration whose pack declares both facets reads back through readDeclaration with its name, pin, library and plugin intact and packsError unset; the renderer's both-facets shape and iklib's library-only shape both read.

A contract-8 declaration that names packs is refused with "packs requires contract 9", never as an unknown key, and its formats still read; a contract past the ceiling is refused whole and the refusal names the contracts that are supported.

A pin is a spoken version and a checked revision: a 40- or 64-character lowercase hex digest is accepted and a branch, a tag, a short prefix, an uppercase digest and an over-long string are each refused by name, because a version alone is a claim rather than a pin.

Each refusal is by name and specific: a facet key under the wrong facet says which facet owns it, a pack with no facet, a repeated pack name, an escaping library.path or plugin.module, and poweredBy on a plugin-only pack each name the pack and the key. A pack with no name is placed by its index and never printed as undefined.

D24 stays as written: poweredBy is accepted on a library facet and refused on a plugin-only pack, so an editor plugin does not earn the claim. It names the pack the claim rests on and asserts nothing about the game integration checks, whose evidence is F21/F29.

A declaration that does not name packs is unchanged: a document carrying all ten blocks of contracts 1-8 reads with the same keys, the same values and no new ones, and packs cannot leak into a result that never asked for it.

Nothing in this feature acquires, downloads, unpacks, loads or interprets a pack. The block carries no URL, registry or fetch step, the reader opens neither library.path nor plugin.module, and plugin.abi is shape-checked and never parsed, ordered or compared. Acquisition stays with KI-008, loading with D38's own spec, editions with D40.

Each regression was observed failing for its own reason: fourteen sabotages, including D24 inverted onto the plugin facet, a tag accepted as a revision, the block never reaching its section and the block leaking into a declaration that never named it. features.description: A paste reaches the PTY whole (KI-070): vterm calls the terminal's output callback once per character, and one socket message per character overran the 128-deep outgoing queue, so everything past roughly the first 128 characters of a paste was dropped in silence and the JSON-per-character churn made it slow as well. Bytes from one event are gathered and leave together, chunked below the session host's 2 MB frame limit and split only on UTF-8 boundaries.
acceptance_criteria: One input event produces one outgoing message rather than one per character: a multi-byte text burst delivered as a single SDL_TEXTINPUT reports exactly one message carrying every byte, counted through re_terminal_inspect_output.

Every public entry point that can make vterm emit flushes what it produced: event, mouse, release and message each run their handler and then flush, so an early return inside a handler cannot strand bytes.

No message exceeds the session host's maxPayload: the buffer is chunked at 128 KiB, which stays under 2 MB even at JSON escaping's worst-case six characters per byte, so a large paste can never close the socket.
A chunk never begins on a UTF-8 continuation byte, so a split cannot put invalid UTF-8 into the PTY on either side of the cut.
The regression was observed failing for its own reason: with the counters present and the batching removed, a 31-byte burst reports 31 messages instead of 1.

F154 DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED, 2026-09-16: the browser sign-in's callback listener never gave its port back. red_worker::signin owned the TcpListener inside the Pending that `held` keeps for the worker's life and that the five-minute deadline thread keeps a second reference to, so a workspace that signed in ONCE held one of the five registered ports until it closed. The ports cannot be OS-assigned — the provider matches redirect URIs exactly and implements no wildcard — and a machine runs several workspaces, so the fifth sign-in was refused with 'Every sign-in port is busy. Close what is using one and try again' and nothing to close. Found as an intermittent npm test failure, which is what a leak looks like from outside; three earlier runs in the session had failed or cancelled without being captured. The listener is now moved into the thread that accepts on it and nowhere else, so the port is released the moment that thread returns — settled, replaced or timed out — and Pending carries only the address to knock on and the ended flag. Regression: a_finished_sign_in_gives_its_port_back binds the port back after both a settled and a cancelled sign-in, sabotage-verified by reintroducing the second handle (two tests go red). The five port-binding tests now take turns on a shared guard, because racing for five fixed numbers is the same flake one level down.

F159 (the desktop child), 2026-09-16: red_supervisor::desktop is what runtime/desktop.mjs hands a window and the channel it is asked things over. The launch is a contract with the NATIVE side, and its absences carry as much as its values — JavaScript drops an undefined from a spawn environment, so an ordinary desktop has no RENGINE_WINDOW_ID at all while one with no terminal has RENGINE_INITIAL_TERMINAL=""; a port writing "" for both would tell the native side this desktop IS a project window whose id happens to be blank. desktop-launch-corpus.json is recorded by launching a real child through the real launchDesktop and asking it what it RECEIVED, which is the only way to record an absence, and Option is the distinction in Rust. The control channel is one newline-framed JSON request per line with ids counting DOWN from -1 (the desktop numbers its own upward) and every non-JSON line skipped, because a window that printed a warning must not fail the inspection in flight; a window that exits answers everyone waiting rather than leaving them to time out. Six sabotages, each observed failing at its own assertion, including the two that collapse an absence into an empty string and one confirmed by the 5-second timeout it produced. The JavaScript half of the record runs while desktop.mjs does and is sabotage-verified from that side too. cargo test --workspace 314/314, npm test 367/367, ./init.sh green.

F159 (the update job), 2026-09-16: red_supervisor::jobs is the caller-facing half of a layered update — what may be asked for, in what order it is refused, and the status polled afterwards. Completion is kept distinct from acceptance: asking answers 202 with a job id and a sentence naming update_status, because a caller treating the 202 as success would report a failed update as a working one. The refusals are ordered (root, layers, desktop, then whether another update is running) so a caller that named a bad layer AND a foreign desktop gets the same sentence every time rather than whichever check was cheapest; a recovery in flight counts as running, because a worker being put back is the same kind of busy and switching one out from under the process restoring it is what the order prevents. A job never ends in 'recovering' — that word means the switch failed and the previous state is going back, and a caller polling for it would wait on something that is not an outcome. Two wire shapes a translation would have got wrong: an absent desktopId is an absent FIELD rather than a null (JSON.stringify drops an undefined, so a workspace-only job has never carried the key), and the job list keeps the newest thirty-two rather than the first. Five sabotages, each observed failing at its own assertion. The LIMITS sentence and the five status words are checked against supervisor.mjs while it still says them.

F159 (the binary), 2026-09-16: red-supervisor is a PROCESS and it serves. `red-supervisor --state DIR --host URL --host-token TOKEN` binds a loopback port, announces itself on stdout as one JSON line (the shape red-worker announces one layer down), writes runtime.json, starts a worker, answers its own thirteen routes, forwards the rest and tunnels /events and /surface byte for byte. The flags are what startRuntime took as injected functions: --worker, --connector, --desktop, --port, --inspect-ui, --initial. supervisor-cutover.test.mjs drives it against a real session host: the descriptor and its host fields, /health without a credential, the 401 for no credential and for a foreign Origin, the composed /api/state, a forwarded /api/feed (the one route nothing but a worker can serve), the update status shape, the refusals IN ORDER, and a whole layered workspace update — candidate started, checked against this host, switched in, previous worker retired and closed. It passed on the first run; four sabotages confirm it, each observed failing for its own reason: the layers judged before the root, update-status forwarded rather than answered, a foreign Origin accepted, and the previous worker never closed (which went red as 'Timed out: the replaced worker drained and closed'). Nothing is deleted yet: a module retires with its CALLER, and the caller is not yet this binary. cargo test --workspace 335/335, npm test 368/368, ./init.sh green.

F159 (the desktop layer), 2026-09-16: the automation relay and the whole desktop choreography, driven. A supervisor that is a PROCESS cannot hand a test the desktop's pipes, and what made that work in JavaScript was also the answer — the supervisor and the test were already two speakers on one stream, split by the sign of the id (the control channel counts DOWN from -1, the automation protocol counts UP from 1). So the supervisor relays that half rather than owning it: GET /automation?owner=... under --inspect-ui, 101, then newline JSON both ways with nothing interpreted on the way through. fake-desktop.mjs is a window as far as the supervisor is concerned — registers through the workspace, answers the control channel, exits 75 on reload and 0 on close — so the choreography runs without a built native binary: open (which does not answer until the window has REGISTERED, because a supervisor answering on spawn would hand a launcher a window that may never arrive), the same binding reused rather than a second window, the relay, a desktop-layer update with the 75 handshake, and a window that detaches on its own. TWO RULES HAD NO CASE until a sabotage of each passed: reading 75 as a close changed nothing (a window going during an update is Expected and the update checks the code itself, so the Detached branch is only reached by an unsolicited 75 — the fixture grew a detach op), and a detach while an update runs queued a second job with no complaint (two perform threads each believing they were active — driven now by declaring a slow desktop build that holds an update in its prepare phase). Both are sabotage-verified now, with five others. One defect the end-to-end test found that compiled and ran: a heredoc turned \r\n into real newlines inside a Rust byte literal and Rust normalises a CR away, so the relay's 101 was framed with bare LFs and no client could read it. cargo test --workspace 336/336, npm test 370/370, ./init.sh green.

F159 (the cutover and the deletion), 2026-09-16: runtime/supervisor.mjs (434), runtime/windows.mjs (109) and runtime/desktop.mjs (47) are DELETED. ensureRuntime starts red-supervisor — asserted by reading the process table, not by trusting the path it passed — and every suite that drove the module drives the binary through red-supervisor-fixture.mjs, which gives it the shape startRuntime had. THE DEEPEST SUITE FOUND TWO REAL BUGS IN THE ROLLBACK, neither visible in a green run: a replacement window that dies on start was forgotten before the rollback could restore it (the restarted view is a new View and nothing marked it as the update's, so its watcher read the exit as a close and removed it), and a failed PREPARATION could not restore a window that had already gone — which is exactly the keyboard case, where the person's window detaches itself and then the build for its replacement fails. native-updates.spec.mjs passes on the Rust supervisor: three layers at once with an unsaved draft open, a build that fails, a candidate that will not start, a keyboard-driven update that fails, a CLI-driven connector update, and a worker crash with the window reconnecting. F159 (which process gets a SIGTERM), 2026-09-16: red_supervisor::replace is launcher/replace.mjs's decisions — the half that matters, because replacing a session host is the one operation here that signals things a person cares about, and it starts from a descriptor naming a pid on a machine where pids are recycled in minutes. Almost all of it is a refusal to SIGNAL: a pid that is alive but is not a session host, a host serving a different state directory (compared on the RESOLVED path, because a directory reached through a link is the same directory and a string comparison would refuse to replace a host that is ours), and a launcher running inside the workspace it would replace, which would die with the host it signalled halfway through — refused with somewhere else to run it, because 'run it elsewhere' is useless without an elsewhere. The PTY service and the store are deliberately left running (D60/D61): children in ps only because the parent that started them has not exited. Judged against replace-host-corpus.json, 25 cases over the process table the JavaScript's own suite was written against — one workspace's host with a pane three levels inside it, two sibling projects, a supervisor with its worker and desktop, a worktree's preflight host, and a state directory with a space in its name. Matched on the first run; six sabotages, including the one that splits a command line on whitespace and turns that last directory into two, and the one that reverts D60's 'handed over' to 'ended'. The report is recorded because a person reads it while deciding whether their editor is about to vanish. npm test 369/369, cargo test --workspace 339/339.

F159 (one ensure path), 2026-09-16: red_core::descriptor::ensure is the start discipline the session host, the supervisor and every state-directory service share — take a lock, spawn, wait for the thing to publish itself — and service::start_service uses it now instead of its own copy. Writing it found a LIVE DEFECT IN SHIPPED RUST: a lock file is created and THEN written, so for an instant it exists and names nobody, and start_service read that as 'nobody holds it', removed the winner's lock while the winner was still spawning, took it, and spawned a SECOND service. The token ledger, the PTY service and the store all start through that path. The JavaScript did not have this bug — it caught SyntaxError separately from 'missing' and waited — and the port had flattened the two into one .ok(). Only a lock that is readable and names a process that is GONE is reclaimed now. Driven by two callers in one process asserting exactly one start; sabotage-verified three times running, and the lock is kept for a live child that has not published (removing it would let the next caller start a second one beside it) and released for one that died. cargo test --workspace 343/343, npm test 369/369.

F159 CRITERION 3 MET, 2026-09-16: the sidecar request/ensure path is one shared implementation. Four copies of 'is this descriptor mine, and is its process alive?' existed in the Rust tree and each was weaker than red_core::descriptor: red-mcp shelled out to `kill -0` (a process the caller may not signal reads as DEAD, on the path that routes every agent pane's tool calls), service::start_service kept its own lock loop with the unwritten-lock race, and red-agents::bind asked /health and threw the answer away — it would have bound an agent to anything answering on that port. All four are the one now. red-agents takes the red-core dependency its manifest had deliberately avoided; the tradeoff was MEASURED before taking it rather than argued, and no binary in the crate grew. bind's identity check had no case until a sabotage of it passed: the case is a state directory whose descriptor points at a live host and claims another instance — the shape a stale descriptor takes when a port is reused — and binding refuses it with 'alive but unavailable: Sidecar identity mismatch. No second sidecar was started.' Sabotage-verified. npm test 370/370, cargo test --workspace 343/343.

A security boundary was added while building these and is now spec 153 decision 11: these flows take a FILENAME from their caller, and a flow that read whatever it was told to would read any file in the project - the API key lives in a file in a project. Flow::file_in resolves a caller-named file inside a directory the project declared and refuses anything outside it; flows::tests::a_caller_cannot_name_a_file_outside_the_directory_the_project_declared covers ../.jev, an absolute path, an empty name and a directory.

Criterion 1, live: `reformat` turned 16 lines of raw notes into 9 blocks - a title, a stitched paragraph (three hard-wrapped lines joined back into one), a section heading, a three-item ordered list, a fenced shell command, a callout and a closing paragraph. Every word in the output was in the input; the flow chose boundaries and types and the Markdown was assembled in code. One formatting bug was found and fixed in the same run: a list running straight into the next block with no blank line, which every Markdown reader swallows into the last item.

Criterion 2, live, and the candidate set was the bug: asked which tool disambiguated the symbols, the first version answered 'workspace.c' at 0.82 - because its pattern kept only tokens carrying a dot, dash or digit, so `nm` and `atos` were never candidates. A confidence says nothing about a set that never contained the answer. Rebuilt to offer every distinct token minus the words that carry no information, ranked by rarity, the same three questions returned workspace.c 1.00, nm 0.96 and MallocScribble 0.99 from 58 candidates instead of 4. The answer is checked against the offered spans before it is returned, so a value that was not in the document cannot come back.

Criterion 3, live: `dates` read 2026-09-18 out of a document that also names March 3 2027, returning month 9 day 18 year 2026 at confidence 0.60, which is the minimum across the parts used. Every calendar decision is in code: runs::reading::tests::an_impossible_date_is_not_a_date pins that February 30 is refused rather than moved to the nearest real day, and a relative date is returned as its anchor because what `today` means is the caller's to know.

Criterion 4, live: `hazards` on a clean document returned every flag at 0.02-0.03 and severity 0.18; on a document carrying an override attempt, a key-shaped string and a named individual it returned overrides 0.98, credential 0.98, personal 0.98 and severity 2.16. It reports `advisory: true` in its own answer and its note says it is not a security control, which is the vendor's own position - nothing in this workspace decides anything on it.

Criterion 5, live: `featurize` over 6 known-issues rows produced 4 columns from 3 declared questions - a Noul becoming one column and a Score becoming two, its mean level and its spread, because a level the model is torn between is a different observation from one it is sure of and one column cannot say so (runs::reading::tests::a_score_becomes_two_columns...). It emits the matrix and fits nothing: the regressor needs a labelled target this workspace does not have and a gradient-boosting dependency this plugin does not carry.
Criterion 6: all five read the key through Jev::from_state_directory, which refuses by name with the path to put one at.

features.description: The composites NOLF proved, rebuilt from the flows rather than beside them: `prior-art` (chunked sweep with an explicit no-match option, every candidate above the floor kept rather than the argmax alone, then `align` per candidate, plus the report's own three judgements asked in parallel over the same state), `prior-findings` (`find` over a project's lessons and antipatterns), `assert-check` (`evidence-check` swept over a tests tree, surface `action`) and `ki-sweep` (`prior-art` over known-issues rows, surface `action`). Spec 153.
acceptance_criteria: `prior-art` keeps every candidate above the floor rather than one per chunk, which is the change NOLF measured as the difference between two surfaced features and three.
The two sweeps are actions and are not offered to an agent as tools.
A composite reuses the flows rather than reimplementing their questions - observed by changing a gate once and seeing every composite follow.
All four exit 0 with an explanation when the key or the service is absent.
features.deliverable: Four composite flows, and the two sweeps declared as actions rather than agent tools.
evidence: Built 2026-09-19 in src/runs/composite.rs. 50 plugin unit tests, clean build. Every one of the 18 flows in the registry now has a runner, and the guard that counted the unbuilt ones reached zero - the test that replaced it asserts there are none.

Criterion 1, live against rEngine's own 192-feature corpus: `prior-art` on a report describing a page that lists plugins and switches them on and off swept all 192, kept ONE candidate at 0.99 and aligned it at the-same 0.88 - F233, which is exactly that feature. On a report about the paste defect it swept 192 and kept NOTHING, which is the right answer: no feature row describes it. The report's own three judgements ran in parallel with the sweep and cost one request beside it.

Criterion 2: `assert-check` and `ki-sweep` are Surface::Action, pinned by registry::tests::the_expensive_flows_are_actions_rather_than_tools, and flows::tools() returns only tool-surface flows - so neither appears in the computed tool list. rEngine's own declaration now carries four tools (triage, find, prior-art, prior-findings) and two actions, verified through `red-jev flows`.

Criterion 3, the reuse: `prior-art`, `prior-findings` and `ki-sweep` all call retrieval::sweep, and `ki-sweep` calls the same align_each as `prior-art`. The gates are read from one module, so CONFIDENT changed once changes every composite. Live: `prior-findings` answered 'is it safe to keep a second copy of a route table in the server that calls it' with the antipattern written into this repo earlier the same day, at 0.99 with presence 0.93 - over a corpus of 2 entries, which the slug-keyed reader made searchable at all.

Criterion 3, the back-off: `ki-sweep` over three rows returned 0 confident matches and named what to LOOK AT for two of them (F55, F61) rather than naming a feature it was not sure of. A wrong merge costs more than a missed one. composite::tests::a_sweep_verdict_backs_off_rather_than_naming_a_feature_it_is_unsure_of pins the rule.

`assert-check` over 8 of this repo's own tests flagged none, with unevidenced probabilities 0.26-0.54, all below the escalate threshold. Its test finder is covered by composite::tests::tests_are_found_by_the_shapes_these_projects_write_them_in - three test shapes across a tree, with node_modules not swept and an underscored Rust name read as the sentence it is.
Criterion 4: all four read the key through Jev::from_state_directory, which refuses by name with the path to put one at.

The agent-facing instructions were updated for this: they now say the visible tool list IS the project's subset, so an agent does not reason from what Jev could do in general, and the obsolete paragraph about composing requests by hand was removed - agents call flows, which carry the measured question shapes themselves. 3,730 characters against the 4,000 cap.

End to end through the real consumer path 2026-09-19: an agent connecting to this project over red-mcp with the plugin switched OFF sees 39 tools; switched ON it sees 43, and the four added are exactly jev.triage, jev.find, jev.prior-art and jev.prior-findings - the tools this project declared. The two action-surface flows are correctly absent from an agent tool list. The instructions grew by 3,732 characters and carry the sentence telling an agent that its visible tool list IS the subset.

features.description: The NOLF workspace adopts the flow library in place of its four standalone Python tools. Its declaration is written in spec 153 and its prerequisite is a submodule bump: third_party/rengine is pinned at a revision that predates this plugin, so the service its manifest would name is not in that checkout. The subset differs from rEngine's - it declares `antipatterns`, which rEngine has no document for, and `passage-triage`, which it needs because its reports come from strangers at release.
acceptance_criteria: NOLF's pinned rEngine carries the jev plugin and its built service.
NOLF declares its own flows.json and gets exactly that subset, different from rEngine's, offered to an agent.
The four Python tools are either retired or recorded as kept, with a reason either way - two implementations of one judgement is two answers to it.
features.deliverable: A submodule bump in the NOLF workspace, its plugins/jev declaration, and a decision recorded about the Python tools.
evidence: NOLF's pinned rEngine carries the plugin and its built service: third_party/rengine moved 71a243bc -> e8b16dd (NOLF commit 85b86b78), `git submodule update --init --recursive`, and `cargo build` in third_party/rengine/plugins/jev/server produces red-jev in that checkout. One binary, shared by every project that pins it; no copy.

NOLF declares its own subset in plugins/jev/flows.json and gets exactly it. `red-jev flows` run from the NOLF root: prior-art and prior-findings as tools, assert-check and ki-sweep as actions. Different from rEngine's six, which declare find and triage that NOLF has no use for, and lack the `antipatterns` source and the `only` marker that NOLF needs.

Verified through the workspace host's own code rather than the CLI - plugins::tools, ::instructions, ::route and ::call against /Users/alex/nolf-improved: two tools offered as jev.prior-art and jev.prior-findings, 3,756 characters of instructions read out of the pinned checkout with no refusal, the tool routable, and a call answering {reads: yes, probability: 0.84} for 2 requests and $0.0006. Two defects were found doing this and fixed in 7750c27.

The four Python tools are RETIRED, not kept: tools/prior_art.py, tools/prior_findings.py, tools/assert_check.py, tools/ki_sweep.py and tests/test_jev_tools_degrade.py are deleted in NOLF 85b86b78, 1,431 lines. Every caller was retargeted - CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, the field-bugs, nolf-audit and nolf-ki-promote skills, and the typesafe-ai adapter. docs/jev-cookbooks.md is kept deliberately: it is the measurement that decided which cookbooks are worth asking there, and it outlived the code it described.

The declaration proposed in spec 153 was corrected by running it: passage-triage takes a `claim` that is an id IN a corpus, so it cannot triage an incoming report, and the injection question NOLF wanted is inside prior-art already. Spec 153 now records what the project runs on rather than what was proposed for it.
One judgement did not survive and is tracked rather than dropped: KI-132, the report `area` Choice. KI-133 tracks the two sweeps not being declared workspace actions.
Another session was working in that tree throughout; only this task's paths were staged, and its uncommitted files are untouched.

features.description: The NOLF migration is measured rather than reviewed: the fixed comparison set of spec 154 runs through the four standalone Python tools and through the library flows that replace them, and every difference is explained before anything is deleted. The defects that measurement finds are fixed in the library, because they are the library's, not NOLF's - a project adopting these flows next would meet the same ones.
acceptance_criteria: The comparison set runs through both implementations and both sets of answers are recorded, negative controls included.
An id names one entry: a document carrying both an index table and the sections it indexes yields one entry per id, and a regression fails when it yields two.
A corpus entry's summary carries its body and not only its title, and a regression fails when the body is dropped.
The presence question names the query in its instructions and keys its entries by id; the measured effect on a true hit and on the negative controls is recorded.
prior-art aligns a candidate on the dimension riders as well as the relation, so a middle answer says WHICH dimension disagrees.
`red-jev corpus` prints what the reader made of a declared source, so a project can count its entries before it trusts a verdict.
Every flow reports what it cost - requests, input tokens and dollars - not input tokens alone.
features.deliverable: A recorded before/after comparison in docs/evidence/, the library fixes it justifies, and the regressions that hold them.
evidence: The comparison set ran through both implementations on 2026-09-19 against the live service; every number is in docs/evidence/jev-migration-2026-09-19.md. The headline: prior-findings on "rename a build target" answered 0.92 through the Python and 0.49 through the library - "decided before" against "unsure" - on a query both rank LL-001 first for. After the fixes, 0.81-0.83. Negative controls sat at 0.01-0.02 before and after, so the change is separation and not a lift.

An id names one entry: corpus::one_entry_per_id, with an_id_names_one_entry_even_when_a_document_indexes_itself over a document that carries an index table and the sections it indexes. Sabotaged by removing the call - FAILED with left ['LL-1','LL-2','LL-1','LL-2'] against right ['LL-1','LL-2'], and nothing else. NOLF's lessons file read 145 entries before and 83 after.

A document entry's summary carries its body: Entry::snippet now switches on corpus::Shape, with a_document_entry_summarises_its_body_and_an_inventory_row_does_not. Sabotaged by emptying the Document body - FAILED with the heading alone against heading-plus-lesson. The inventory path is unchanged, which is deliberate: 254 descriptions of 120 characters is the sweep both implementations share and it was measured that way.

The presence question names the query in its instructions and keys its entries by id (runs::retrieval::presence). Isolated over four conditions on the same corpus and criteria: generic/list 0.63, generic/keyed 0.77, named/list 0.84, named/keyed 0.91, with the control at 0.01-0.02 throughout. Restoring the body to each summary was worth +0.12 and the second sentence of each criterion +0.06-0.17.

prior-art aligns on the riders as well as the relation: measured on "tree is visible through plants", F1294 reads same-subject 0.83 / same-symptom 0.33 and F1121 reads 0.29 / 0.18 - which is what separates the candidate worth opening from the one that is not. Run cost 11 requests and $0.0029 against the Python's 9 and $0.0028.

`red-jev corpus --flow NAME --source KEY` prints the path, entry count, shape, option budget, the requests a sweep would cost and a sample. It contacts nothing. Run against NOLF's declared lessons: 73 entries, document shape, budget 260.

Every flow reports `cost` as requests, input tokens and dollars, accumulated on the client from the service's own usage field. what_a_run_cost_is_measured_and_not_estimated pins the rate against a run both implementations measured (66,909 tokens, $0.0028); sabotaged to ten times the rate it FAILED with 0.0281 against 0.0028.
Gates: 54 plugin unit tests green, the red workspace green, design.py check, agent_names.py check and features.py validate green.

Two further defects came from pointing the workspace host's own code at the NOLF checkout instead of reading it (7750c27). A computed tool list was offered but not callable - the offer asked the plugin and the routing read the manifest's `tools`, which for such a plugin is the name of a subcommand rather than an array, so route() refused every tool the same plugin had just advertised. Observed failing first: a_computed_tool_is_callable_and_not_only_listed panicked at 'a tool an agent is offered is a tool it can reach' before the fix. And a manifest's `instructions` resolved from the plugin's own directory while `command` resolved from the project root, so a project pinning the plugin had nowhere to point at the prose that belongs with the service; now both resolve from the project root with `..` and absolute still refused.

A third came from looking at what CALLED the tool being replaced (953cd97): a promotion skill ran `ki_sweep.py --ki KI-NNN` against one row, and the flow replacing it could only sweep the first N of a list. `ki-sweep --row KI-494` on NOLF: 11 requests, $0.003, ranking F1584 first - the feature that row's own second cell names - against $0.95 for the list.

A sweep is about the rows the project says are live, and the two projects say it in opposite directions: NOLF writes `major (OPEN - ...)` in a severity cell and declares `settings.only: "OPEN"`; rEngine's rows say nothing when open and open with `**Closed YYYY-MM-DD.**` when done, so it declares `settings.except: "**Closed"`, which takes its sweep from 126 rows to 115. Observed failing for its own reason: with the filter stubbed to accept everything, a_sweep_is_about_the_rows_the_project_declared_it_is_about FAILED with ['KI-1','KI-2'] against ['KI-2'].
Gates: 54 plugin unit tests, 80 red-project tests, the red workspace green, npm 380/380, ./init.sh, design.py check, agent_names.py check and features.py validate green.

features.description: The transferable half: a runbook another project follows to adopt the flow library, and the retirement of NOLF's four Python tools once their replacements are measured. What the Python did and the library does not is tracked as work rather than kept as a second implementation.
acceptance_criteria: A runbook in docs/runbooks/ takes a project from no plugin to a declared subset answering, in steps that name commands rather than describing them.
The four Python tools and their degrade test are gone from NOLF, and its AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and cookbook record point at the flows instead.
Everything the Python did that the library does not is a tracked row or a known issue, with the measurement behind it - nothing is dropped silently.
The insights the migration produced are recorded where the next project reads them, not only in this spec.
features.deliverable: docs/runbooks/jev-project-adoption.md, the removal commit in the NOLF workspace, and the follow-up rows for what did not survive.
evidence: docs/runbooks/jev-project-adoption.md takes a project from no plugin to a declared subset answering, in six numbered steps that name commands: pin and build, declare flows.json, declare plugin.json, switch on and key, verify in the order that catches the silent failure first (`corpus` before anything, because a reader that made 145 entries out of 75 still answers), and only then retire what it replaces.

The retirement protocol is the part that transfers: fix the comparison set before starting, include at least two inputs the corpus cannot answer, run both, and allow only three outcomes for a difference - fix the library, record it as deliberate, or track the capability as not surviving. The five traps are listed so the next project checks for them rather than finding them.

NOLF 85b86b78: the four tools and the degrade test are gone, and CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, the field-bugs / nolf-audit / nolf-ki-promote skills and the typesafe-ai adapter all point at the flows. A skill telling an agent to run a deleted script is a broken skill, so each call site was rewritten rather than annotated.

What did not survive is tracked, not dropped: KI-132 (the report `area` judgement, because `classify` takes a subject that is already an id in a corpus) and KI-133 (the two sweeps are not declared workspace actions, so `dashboard_actions` does not offer them).

The insight is recorded where the next project reads it: docs/lessons-learned.md, 'a port is not a migration until the same inputs give the same answer', with what each of the five defects cost and why a review cannot catch any of them.
